section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Laparoscopic Gastrectomy for Gastric Cancer
section.intro: Laparoscopic gastrectomy is a minimally invasive way to remove part or all of the stomach affected by gastric cancer. These FAQs explain how the surgery works, who may be suitable, what recovery involves, and how international patients can plan treatment.

items.q: What is laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer?
items.a: Laparoscopic gastrectomy is minimally invasive surgery that removes part or all of the stomach affected by gastric cancer through several small incisions instead of one large cut. A thin camera and specialised instruments guide the surgeon, who also removes nearby lymph nodes for staging. It aims to remove the tumour completely while reducing surgical trauma. Whether it is suitable depends on cancer stage, tumour location, and specialist review of your reports.

items.q: How is laparoscopic gastrectomy different from open surgery?
items.a: Laparoscopic gastrectomy uses several small keyhole incisions, while open surgery uses one large abdominal incision. Both aim to remove the cancer and affected lymph nodes, but the minimally invasive approach often means less blood loss, smaller scars, and a shorter hospital stay for selected patients. Open surgery may still be preferred for larger or more advanced tumours. The final choice depends on your tumour and surgical team's assessment.

items.q: What are the types of laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: The main types are laparoscopic distal gastrectomy, which removes the lower stomach, and laparoscopic total gastrectomy, which removes the entire stomach. Some patients may have a proximal or subtotal gastrectomy depending on where the tumour sits. Each type is paired with lymph node removal for accurate staging. The type chosen depends on tumour location, size, stage, and the surgeon's evaluation, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What are the benefits of minimally invasive gastrectomy?
items.a: The main benefits of minimally invasive gastrectomy are smaller incisions, less pain, reduced blood loss, and often a faster return to normal activity for selected patients. Many people experience a shorter hospital stay and quicker recovery of bowel function compared with open surgery. Cancer-control outcomes can be comparable in suitable early-stage cases. Actual benefits vary by patient, tumour stage, and surgical experience, and should be reviewed with your treating team.

items.q: Who is eligible for laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: Laparoscopic gastrectomy may be considered mainly for early and selected locally advanced gastric cancers where the tumour can be removed completely. Suitability depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous abdominal surgery, overall fitness, and specialist review. Patients with very advanced disease, extensive spread, or certain anatomical factors may be advised open surgery instead. Final eligibility should be decided by the treating surgical and oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: How is a laparoscopic gastrectomy performed?
items.a: During laparoscopic gastrectomy, the surgeon makes several small incisions and inserts a camera and instruments to view and operate inside the abdomen. The affected part of the stomach and nearby lymph nodes are removed, and the digestive tract is reconnected so food can pass through. The procedure is done under general anaesthesia and usually takes a few hours. Exact steps depend on the type of resection and each patient's anatomy.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: Like any major surgery, laparoscopic gastrectomy carries risks such as bleeding, infection, leakage at the join in the digestive tract, and reactions to anaesthesia. Longer-term effects can include changes in eating, weight loss, dumping syndrome, and vitamin deficiencies, especially after total gastrectomy. Most side effects are manageable with dietary support and follow-up. Individual risk depends on health, stage, and surgical complexity, and should be discussed with your treating team.

items.q: How long is recovery after laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: Recovery after laparoscopic gastrectomy is often quicker than open surgery, with many selected patients leaving hospital within about five to ten days. Eating usually restarts gradually with small, frequent meals guided by a dietitian. Returning to normal activity can take several weeks, and full digestive adjustment may take longer, especially after total gastrectomy. Recovery time varies with age, overall health, and whether additional treatment is needed, so timelines should be individualised.

items.q: How much does laparoscopic gastrectomy cost?
items.a: The cost of laparoscopic gastrectomy varies widely by country, hospital, and the type of resection performed. It typically includes surgery, hospital stay, anaesthesia, investigations, and follow-up care, and may rise if complications occur or additional treatment is required. Costs are often lower in India and some Asian centres than in Western countries. Final pricing depends on your diagnosis, stage, tests, protocol, and length of stay, so a personalised estimate is recommended.

items.q: Is laparoscopic gastrectomy available in India?
items.a: Laparoscopic gastrectomy is available at several major cancer and surgical centres in India, where experienced upper-gastrointestinal surgeons perform minimally invasive and robotic procedures. Many centres also offer combined care with medical and radiation oncology teams. Availability and suitability depend on the hospital, tumour stage, and specialist evaluation of your reports. International patients often choose India for experienced teams and comparatively lower costs, but acceptance always depends on medical review.

items.q: Which countries offer laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer?
items.a: Laparoscopic gastrectomy is offered in many countries with established gastric cancer programmes, including India, China, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and across Europe and North America. East Asian centres have particularly high volumes because gastric cancer is common there. The best option depends on cancer stage, surgical expertise, cost, and travel practicality. Choosing a centre should be based on medical review, surgeon experience, and discussion with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What is robotic gastrectomy and how does it compare?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is a form of minimally invasive surgery where the surgeon controls robotic arms with enhanced precision and a magnified three-dimensional view. It may help with detailed lymph node removal and complex reconstructions in selected patients. Compared with standard laparoscopy, it can offer greater dexterity but usually costs more and requires specialised equipment. Whether it offers a meaningful advantage depends on the case and should be discussed with your surgical team.

items.q: Is laparoscopic surgery used for advanced gastric cancer?
items.a: Laparoscopic surgery is used mainly for early and selected locally advanced gastric cancers, and its role in more advanced disease is still being studied. For advanced tumours, surgery is often combined with chemotherapy before or after the operation, and open surgery may sometimes be safer. Some centres offer minimally invasive resection in carefully chosen advanced cases. The approach depends on staging, response to prior treatment, and multidisciplinary specialist review.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for minimally invasive gastric cancer surgery?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study laparoscopic and robotic gastrectomy, including their use in locally advanced disease and combined with newer chemotherapy or immunotherapy regimens. Trials may compare minimally invasive and open surgery for long-term outcomes. Participation does not guarantee benefit, and eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment against strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Ask your oncology team whether a relevant trial may be appropriate for you.

items.q: What reports are needed to plan laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: Planning laparoscopic gastrectomy usually requires an endoscopy report with biopsy confirming gastric cancer, CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and staging investigations such as a PET scan where advised. Blood tests, fitness assessments, and sometimes diagnostic laparoscopy help confirm suitability. Sharing complete and recent reports helps the surgical team assess whether minimally invasive surgery is appropriate. The exact tests required depend on your case and treating centre.

items.q: Will I need chemotherapy before or after laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: Many patients with gastric cancer receive chemotherapy before or after surgery to improve control of the disease, though this is not the same for everyone. Treatment before surgery can shrink the tumour, while treatment afterwards targets any remaining cancer cells. The need for chemotherapy depends on stage, tumour biology, and overall health. This is decided by a multidisciplinary team, and final treatment decisions should be made by your treating oncology team.

items.q: What follow-up care is needed after gastrectomy?
items.a: Follow-up after gastrectomy typically includes regular clinical reviews, nutritional support, and periodic scans or endoscopy to monitor for recurrence. Because the stomach's role in digestion changes, patients often need dietary guidance and vitamin or mineral supplements, especially vitamin B12 after total gastrectomy. Ongoing oncology follow-up helps manage any further treatment. The exact schedule depends on stage, surgery type, and recovery, and should be arranged with your treating medical team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with laparoscopic gastrectomy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant surgical specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Access to any hospital or procedure depends on medical review, hospital acceptance, and travel fitness. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health, and no outcome or acceptance is guaranteed.
